prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a genuine invention that opened a door: the magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift and motional errors, and it has been realised experimentally by several independent laboratories with mutually consistent comparisons at the 10^-18 level. It satisfies my own test of an original experiment that is verified and matters for our understanding of nature (tests of constants, relativistic geodesy, the coming redefinition of the second). My opening ballot placed it second; after reading the opening ballots I see it is the one candidate that six of eight colleagues placed in their top three and that nobody ranked below seventh, and the attribution is the cleanest on the list: Katori proposed the scheme and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye drove it to record accuracy and stability. A two-person prize leaves room for no arbitrary exclusions inside a collaboration, which is the problem that haunts several other candidates.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is my own stated criterion: the prize should reward the original work and not the second group that did it much better. Ye's decisive contribution is performance and the many-body clock, built on frequency-comb and laser-cooling prizes already awarded (2005, 1997, 2012), so the committee must be certain that Katori's invention, not Ye's refinement, is what we are crediting, and that the citation reflects this. There is also a legitimate objection that the advance is incremental relative to those earlier metrology prizes, and that other groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Derevianko on theory) are left out. If the committee views these as decisive, my own first-ranked B015, the aberration corrector, or the Higgs experiments would be the alternatives.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a textbook case of a new measurement technique that moves the precision frontier by orders of magnitude, with two laureates a clean and fair configuration, while noting overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and with the maturity assessment, and it is the reason I moved the clock to the head of my configuration. I would qualify the overlap point more firmly than you do: we should write the citation around the lattice-trapping invention and its realisation, not around accuracy records, so that it is clearly distinct from the frequency comb and ion-clock prizes and does not read as a lifetime award to Ye. I also disagree gently that squeezed light or NV sensing offer comparable clarity, since their credit is far more diffuse.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as detector-driven discovery that opened a new observational window, and ranks the Higgs experiments second, accepting that allocation among spokespersons and founders is contested.
responses.response: I share your valuation of detector-driven discoveries; I ranked IceCube fourth for that reason. My reservation is about what is verified at the level of the credited names: the diffuse flux is solid, but source identification (TXS 0506+056, the Galactic plane) is statistically modest, and you yourself say you cannot independently verify the relative shares of Halzen, Karle and Spiering, nor the roles of AMANDA and Baikal pioneers. I would be more comfortable with IceCube in a later year, once the sources are firmer. On the Higgs, the allocation problem you describe is real and, in my view, argues against it this year rather than for a rushed three-name choice.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, as experiment overturning theoretical expectation that created a tunable platform, and places aberration-corrected electron optics fourth while asking whether it counts as physics or instrumentation.
responses.response: Thank you for ranking B015 and for naming the physics-versus-chemistry question openly; I do think sub-angstrom imaging is physics, since it is the optics of electrons, but I accept that this is a real question and that my own field makes me an interested party. On twisted bilayer graphene I remain more cautious than you: I ranked it last, not because the discovery is not striking, but because the superconducting mechanism is still debated, the field is under a decade old, and the experimental credit among Cao, Jarillo-Herrero, Dean and Efetov groups is not settled by the supplied names. I would want that field to settle first; the clock does not have that problem.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture for a new light-matter regime, while admitting that superconducting circuits were recognised recently and that credit boundaries with the Yale group are unclear.
responses.response: The science is clearly strong, but I side with your own caveat. A return to superconducting circuits so soon after the recent award, with the Yale credit boundaries unsettled, makes B054 harder to defend than a clock prize in an area the prize has not covered for this specific achievement. I would want the committee to be sure, in the words I use for every candidate, that we have found the people doing the original work.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye are credited for the same achievement or the committee should treat lattice proposal and record-accuracy realisation as separate contributions with a different order of merit.
Whether the lack of any credit for Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or Derevianko would be judged as unfair to other groups.
Whether the aberration-corrector (B015) is considered physics by the committee and how the Krivanek and Dellby priority on the STEM corrector affects the credited trio.
Whether the committee prefers a different year for the redefinition-of-the-second context, since the SI redefinition is still pending.
statement.conflict_note: One connection requires a conflict check: B015 is in my own field, electron microscopy, and I know the aberration-corrected TEM and STEM community through the IFSM and my own work, so I would consider recusing myself from any decision on B015. I also share an institution (Chalmers) with Göran Johansson, whose first-ranked candidate is B054. No specific conflict is apparent for B013 or the other shortlisted candidates from the provided profile.
